lessons.title: Wash, Wash, Wash Your Hands
objectives: Wash hands with soap in the right steps
Know when to wash hands
prerequisites: Can use a tap with help
explanation: Germs are tiny living things too small to see. Some can make us sick. They get on our hands when we play, use the toilet or touch animals.
Washing with soap and water removes germs. Wet your hands, rub with soap — palms, backs, between fingers, under nails — for about 20 seconds (sing "Happy Birthday" twice), rinse and dry.
Wash before eating, after using the toilet, after playing outside, and after touching animals. Cover coughs and sneezes with your elbow.

vocabulary.meaning: tiny living things that can make us sick
helps wash germs away

examples: Washing hands before eating dal and rice.

story.title: The Germ Party That Didn't Happen
story.text: Tiny germs were planning a party on Kiko's hands after Kiko played in the mud. "Lunch time! We'll jump into the food!" they giggled. But Kiko went to the sink, scrubbed with soap and sang "Happy Birthday" twice. Whoosh! The germs washed away. Party cancelled!

lessons.title: My Body, My Rules
objectives: Name private parts as the parts covered by a swimsuit
Know to say no, get away, and tell a trusted adult about unsafe touch
explanation: Your body belongs to you. Private parts are the parts covered by a swimsuit. Nobody should touch your private parts, or ask you to touch theirs, except a parent or doctor helping keep you clean or healthy — and a doctor only with your parent there.
Safe touch feels good and caring, like a hug from family you want. Unsafe touch makes you feel scared, confused or uncomfortable. You can always say "No!", move away, and tell a trusted grown-up.

Trusted grown-ups are people who keep you safe, like parents, grandparents or a teacher. Surprises (like a birthday present) are fun, but secrets that make you feel bad should always be told — even if someone says not to. It is never your fault.

vocabulary.meaning: the parts of the body covered by a swimsuit

touch that feels scary or wrong

examples: A high-five from a friend: safe touch.

story.title: Momo's Helping Hand
story.text: Momo made a "helping hand" by tracing a paw on paper. On each finger, Momo wrote the name of a trusted grown-up: Mama, Papa, Grandma, Teacher, Aunty Tara. "If I ever feel unsafe or have a worry," Momo said, "I can tell any of these five. And if one doesn't listen, I'll tell the next."

lessons.title: Stop, Look and Listen
objectives: Explain how to cross a road safely with an adult
Know the meaning of traffic light colours
explanation: Roads can be dangerous because vehicles move fast. Always hold a grown-up's hand near roads, and walk on the footpath.

To cross: find a safe place like a zebra crossing or a green pedestrian signal. Stop at the edge. Look right, left and right again (in India, traffic drives on the left). Listen for vehicles. Cross when it's clear, walking straight across.
Traffic lights: red means stop, amber (yellow) means get ready, green means go — but still look! In a car, always wear a seat belt or sit in a child seat. On a two-wheeler, wear a helmet.

vocabulary.meaning: black and white stripes where people cross
a person walking
a strap that keeps you safe in a car
a hard hat that protects your head

examples: Waiting for the green walking signal.
Wearing a helmet on a scooter.

story.title: Kiko Learns to Wait
story.text: Kiko saw a friend across the busy road and wanted to run! Tara held Kiko back. "Stop. Look. Listen." A bus whooshed past. They walked to the zebra crossing, waited for the green signal, looked both ways, and crossed together. "Patience keeps us safe," said Tara.

activities.prompt: We should wear a seat belt in a car.

lessons.title: Danger Detectives at Home
objectives: Identify common dangers at home
Know how to get help in an emergency
explanation: Homes are mostly safe, but some things can hurt us: hot stoves and irons, sharp knives, medicines and cleaning liquids, electric sockets, and open windows or balconies.
Never touch medicines or cleaning bottles without a grown-up. Never put anything into sockets. Stay away from the stove unless a grown-up is helping.
In an emergency, find a grown-up. In India, 112 is the emergency number for police, fire and ambulance. Learn your full name, your parent's name, phone number and address.

context.text: India's Emergency Response Support System uses 112 as a single emergency number; 1098 is the CHILDLINE number for children in need of help.

vocabulary.meaning: something that can hurt you
a sudden dangerous situation
something to treat illness, only given by adults

examples: A pan handle turned inward so no one knocks it.

lessons.title: Fresh and Clean Every Day
objectives: Follow a daily personal hygiene routine
Explain how hygiene prevents illness
explanation: Personal hygiene means keeping your body clean. Bathe daily, especially in hot weather when you sweat. Brush teeth twice a day.
Keep nails short and clean, since germs hide under them. Wash and comb your hair. Wear clean clothes and socks.
Use the toilet properly, flush or pour water, and wash hands afterwards. Good hygiene prevents infections and helps you feel confident.

vocabulary.meaning: keeping clean to stay healthy

objectives: Explain what to do if there is a fire

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Get Out, Stay Out
objectives: Explain what to do if there is a fire
Follow water safety rules
explanation: If there is a fire, get out quickly and stay out. Don't stop to collect toys. If there is smoke, crawl low where the air is cleaner. Before opening a door, feel it with the back of your hand — if hot, use another way.
Once outside, call 112 or tell a grown-up, and never go back inside. If your clothes catch fire: Stop, Drop and Roll to put out the flames.
Water is fun but can be dangerous. Only swim with a grown-up watching. Never go into rivers, lakes, the sea or wells alone, and stay away from deep water in the monsoon.

vocabulary.meaning: dark gas from fire that is harmful to breathe

to be harmed by being unable to breathe under water

examples: Practising a family fire drill with a meeting point.

story.title: The Family Fire Drill
story.text: Zuri's family practised a fire drill. Papa pressed the smoke alarm test button — BEEP! Everyone crawled low to the door, went outside and met at the big neem tree. "Two minutes!" said Mama. "Now we know exactly what to do if it ever happens."

activities.prompt: Only swim when a grown-up is watching.

lessons.title: Be a First Aider
objectives: Treat minor cuts, burns and nosebleeds safely
Know when to call for adult or medical help
explanation: First aid is the first help given to an injured person. For a small cut: wash with clean water, press gently with a clean cloth to stop bleeding, and cover with a plaster. Tell an adult.
For a burn: cool it under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Don't put ice, butter, toothpaste or oil on it. Get adult help.

For a nosebleed: sit up, lean forward (not back), and pinch the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes. For anything serious — bad bleeding, someone not responding, trouble breathing — call 112 and get an adult immediately.

vocabulary.meaning: the first help given to someone injured or ill

examples: A grazed knee washed and covered.

story.title: The Playground Fall
story.text: Ravi fell and scraped his knee. Asha stayed calm: "Let's tell the teacher." Together they rinsed the graze with clean water, pressed it with a clean tissue, and the teacher put on a plaster. "You were a great first aider," the teacher told Asha.

activities.prompt: For serious injuries, call 112 and get an adult.

lessons.title: Keep It Private
objectives: Identify personal information that should be kept private online
Know what to do if something online feels wrong
explanation: Personal information includes your full name, address, school, phone number, passwords and photos showing where you live. Keep these private online, just like you wouldn't tell a stranger on the street.
People online may not be who they say they are. Never agree to meet someone you only know online, and never send photos to strangers.
If anything online makes you feel worried, scared or uncomfortable — a message, picture or request — stop, don't reply, and tell a trusted adult. You won't be in trouble for telling.

vocabulary.meaning: details that identify you
a secret code to protect an account
someone you only know through the internet
keeping your information safe

examples: A game asking for your home address — don't share it.

story.text: While playing an online game, someone called "CoolKid12" asked Nova which school Nova went to and for a photo. Nova felt uneasy and remembered the rule: stop, don't reply, tell. Nova told Papa, who blocked and reported the account. "You did exactly the right thing," Papa said.

lessons.title: Boundaries and Consent
objectives: Explain consent in everyday situations
Practise setting and respecting boundaries
prerequisites: Knows body safety and trusted adults
explanation: Boundaries are limits people set about what feels okay — for touch, personal space, belongings and information. Everyone's boundaries can be different, and they can change.

Consent means freely agreeing to something. It should be clear and can be withdrawn at any time. Asking "Is it okay if I…?" and respecting "no" are signs of respect — in hugs, borrowing things, sharing photos, and games.
Peer pressure can push people to cross boundaries. It's okay to say no firmly. If anyone pressures, threatens or harms you, tell a trusted adult or call CHILDLINE 1098.

vocabulary.meaning: a limit about what feels okay to you
freely given permission
influence from people your age to do something
treating others' choices as important

examples: Asking before posting a photo of a friend.
Saying "I don't want to play that game" and walking away.

story.title: The Photo Question
story.text: At a birthday party, Meera took a funny photo of Arjun mid-sneeze and was about to post it to the class group. She paused and asked, "Is it okay if I share this?" Arjun laughed but said, "Please don't." Meera deleted it. Arjun trusted her even more after that.

activities.prompt: Before sharing a photo of a friend, you should…

lessons.title: Making a Good Emergency Call
objectives: Describe the steps of responding to an emergency
Make a clear emergency call
explanation: In an emergency, first check for Danger — don't get hurt yourself. Then check Response: speak loudly and tap the person's shoulders. Shout for help.
Call 112 (or ask someone to). Say clearly: what happened, where you are (address and landmarks), how many people are hurt, and their condition. Don't hang up until told to.

If someone is not breathing normally, trained people give CPR (chest compressions). If someone is breathing but unresponsive, the recovery position helps keep the airway open. Learning first aid from a certified course is valuable.

a safe side-lying position for an unconscious breathing person
a well-known place used to give directions
someone who helps in an emergency

A school first aid course for older students.

story.title: The Calm Caller
story.text: When Grandmother fainted in the kitchen, eleven-year-old Kabir checked that the floor was safe, called her name loudly and tapped her shoulders. She was breathing but not answering. He called 112 and gave the address and landmark slowly and clearly. The ambulance arrived quickly. The paramedic said his clear call had saved precious minutes.

lessons.title: Hazard, Risk and Decisions
objectives: Distinguish hazard from risk
Use a simple risk matrix and recognise biases in risk perception
prerequisites: Knows safety rules and probability basics
explanation: A hazard is something that could cause harm (a busy road). Risk is the chance that harm will happen and how bad it would be. Risk = likelihood × severity.
A risk matrix rates likelihood and severity to prioritise actions. Controls reduce risk: eliminate, substitute, add barriers, train people, and use protective equipment.

People often misjudge risk: dramatic rare events (like plane crashes) feel scarier than common ones (like road accidents). In India, road crashes cause well over a hundred thousand deaths each year, many involving two-wheelers and pedestrians — so helmets, seat belts and safe speeds save many lives.

context.text: Government of India road accident reports record around 1.5 lakh or more deaths annually in recent years.

vocabulary.meaning: something that could cause harm
likelihood and severity of harm
an action that reduces risk
judging risk by how easily examples come to mind

examples: Wearing a helmet reduces the severity of head injuries.
A guard rail on a balcony is a barrier control.

story.title: The Scary Headline
story.text: After a rare shark attack made the news, many people stopped swimming at the beach — but continued riding scooters without helmets. A student compared the numbers. "We fear what's dramatic, not what's dangerous," she wrote in her school magazine.

lessons.title: Health for Everyone
objectives: Explain major public health measures and their impact
Discuss mental health and help-seeking as part of public health
explanation: Public health protects the health of whole populations through clean water and sanitation, vaccination, disease surveillance, health education and safe environments.
During epidemics, measures like testing, contact tracing, isolation and vaccination slow spread. They work best when people trust and cooperate with them.

Mental health is part of health. Stress, anxiety and depression are common and treatable. Talking to trusted people and professionals is a sign of strength. In India, Tele-MANAS (14416) provides free mental health support.

context.text: The National Tele Mental Health Programme (Tele-MANAS) was launched in 2022 with the toll-free number 14416.

vocabulary.meaning: protecting health of whole populations
a rapid spread of disease in a population
finding people exposed to an infected person

examples: Mass polio vaccination campaigns.
School counsellors supporting students' wellbeing.

story.title: The Polio Volunteers
story.text: For years, thousands of health workers and volunteers walked village to village, crossing rivers and climbing hills to give polio drops to every child — sometimes many times. In 2014, India was certified polio-free. Public health, one doctor said, is "millions of small actions adding up".
